problems.memo_sentence: The authors claim that their Hamiltonian-simulation-based algorithm achieves expected accuracy levels comparable to classical numerical algorithms for the Black–Scholes PDE while using 9 qubits on a fault-tolerant quantum computer, and they present convergence and relative discretization-error studies versus the analytical solution for different numbers of qubits.
problems.source_evidence: “We report expected accuracy levels comparable to classical numerical algorithms by using 9 qubits to simulate its dynamics on a fault-tolerant quantum computer...” and later “The simulations show a precision comparable to classical algorithms with a quantum circuit comprising 9 qubits to simulate the dynamics of the PDE in a fault-tolerant quantum computer...” The paper also says “the numerical method proposed in this manuscript relies on the Black-Scholes model in order to show its properties of convergence and accuracy.”
problems.explanation: The memo presents the 9-qubit result as a demonstrated algorithmic achievement, but the paper frames it as an expected accuracy level / simulation result rather than a validated end-to-end quantum implementation. It also omits that the paper uses the Black-Scholes model specifically to illustrate convergence and accuracy properties.

problems.memo_sentence: The authors explicitly confine their contribution to the Hamiltonian simulation subroutine and state that they do not attempt to address the full end-to-end option-pricing workflow, highlighting that their work covers only one component of a broader pricing pipeline.
problems.source_evidence: The paper says: “our manuscript focuses on the Hamiltonian simulation step as a subroutine to solve the option pricing problem and does not aim to discuss the end-to-end process of such a task.” It also adds: “In order to achieve this practical task in an efficient way, one can follow the methodology described in [71] ... Finally it is possible to efficiently compute the expected value of the price under the distribution of the stock for obtaining the pricing of the derivative.”
problems.explanation: The memo captures the subroutine-only scope, but it misses the explicit statement that full pricing requires an additional methodology beyond the Hamiltonian simulation step. That omission matters because the paper is careful that the presented algorithm is not the complete pricing pipeline.

problems.memo_sentence: The authors propose extending their embedding-and-post-selection framework to more complex non-Hermitian PDEs in finance, including models with spatial–time-dependent (stochastic local) volatility and coupled options, as well as moving beyond European options to simulate American and Asian options.
problems.source_evidence: The paper says: “This could allow us to introduce additional degrees of freedom in the model, e.g. spatial-time dependent volatility (stochastic local volatility) or coupled options. For instance, we could use the quantum principal component analysis raised in Ref. [12] together with coupled Black-Scholes models to address problems with coupled options. Moreover, the present work has been accomplished for the European option pricing problem, but it may be carried through simulate different kind of options, considering American and Asian options [45], for example.”
problems.explanation: The memo turns speculative future directions into a firmer proposal. The source uses cautious language (“could,” “may be carried through”), so the memo slightly overstates the certainty of these extensions.

problems.memo_sentence: The paper claims to introduce a digital quantum algorithm that directly solves the Black–Scholes option-pricing PDE by mapping it to a Schrödinger equation and employing efficient Hamiltonian simulation techniques—specifically QSP-based sparse simulation—rather than Monte Carlo sampling approaches that assume known dynamics.
problems.source_evidence: The paper states: “Our approach differs from those based on Monte Carlo integration, exclusively focused on sampling the solution assuming the dynamics is known.” It also cites prior work on QSP and sparse Hamiltonian simulation in refs. [70] and [56], rather than presenting QSP as a novel contribution of this paper.
problems.explanation: The paper’s novelty is the application of Hamiltonian simulation to Black-Scholes, not the invention of QSP-based sparse simulation itself. The memo attributes the QSP-based technique too directly to this paper instead of recognizing it as an imported method from cited literature.
